paras: The lynching of Franklin Baker was the hanging of a Colorado homesteader by a mob at Cheyenne Wells in April 1888, after he was arrested for shooting two land seekers who crossed his claim. Officers were moving him toward Denver when the mob, put at fifty men, took him and hanged him to a railroad coal chute. The case ran in papers from Washington to California, first as a shooting and a promised lynching, then as brief notices of the hanging.

According to a Cheyenne Wells wire of April 16, N. B. McConnell and John Morrison, two young men from Iowa, were driving past Baker's house on Saturday, April 14, when he ordered them to stop. When they kept going, he fired a shotgun loaded with slugs or buckshot into the wagon; the driver was unhurt. A Denver dispatch said Baker's wife told him to shoot, and quoted Baker as saying "he did not want anybody driving over his land." Reports of the victims' fate differed: the first wire said both died within five minutes, while other reports said they were not expected to live, or that one had died.

Baker was arrested, and on the night the wire was sent fifty armed men went to the jail and demanded him from the deputy sheriff. The deputy refused, but the men said they would hang Baker before morning "if they have to tear the jail down." A telegram from Burlington to the Denver News said Baker was strongly guarded to keep the citizens from taking the law into their own hands.

According to a dispatch from Wallace, Kansas, dated April 18, threats of lynching led officers to move Baker from Burlington to Cheyenne Wells, meaning to take him on to Denver for safekeeping. There, on the evening of April 17, a mob seized him and "hung him to the coal chute." Other accounts said the mob overpowered his guards, took him from the sheriff, or acted "in spite of the resistance of the officers."

Baker's wife was arrested as an accessory to the shooting, and the Wallace dispatch reported threats to lynch her as well. No report of an inquest, of arrests of mob members, or of the outcome of the wife's case appears in the coverage.

The first wire ran on April 17 under headlines that predicted the lynching, such as the Salt Lake Herald's "They're Determined to Lynch Him" and the Silver State's "The Perpetrator Probably Lynched." The Sacramento Record-Union called the shooting "The Act of a Fiend" by "a Colorado Brute," while the Washington Evening Star headed it "Wantonly Shot Down." No report gave a race for Baker, his victims or the mob.

Reports of the hanging were short items in Dakota, Kansas, Colorado and Montana papers, under headings such as "Strung Up to a Coal Chute" and "Lynch Law." The Thomas County Cat in Kansas titled its account "Terrible Tragedy-Swift Justice," and the local Bent County Register reasoned that there was probably no cause for the shooting, "or mob violence would not have been used." The Salt Lake Herald, writing before news of the hanging, took the other side, saying the determination to lynch Baker showed that "western civilization has not reached the proper status of Christian civilization."

The papers disagreed on Baker's first name, given as Franklin, Frederick or Fred, and on the county, given as Bent in the Wallace dispatch and Elbert in the Thomas County Cat. Dates also varied: some reports put the lynching on the night of the shooting, but wires of April 16 and 17 still described Baker as alive under guard, which fits the Wallace dispatch's date of April 17. Accounts of his wife's role ranged from telling him to shoot to handing him the gun.

framing.detail: The April 16 wire ran under headlines anticipating the lynching: 'They're Determined to Lynch Him', 'Will Be Lynched', 'The Perpetrator Probably Lynched'.
The Sacramento Record-Union headed the shooting 'The Act of a Fiend' by 'a Colorado Brute', and the Thomas County Cat headed the hanging 'Terrible Tragedy-Swift Justice'.
The Bent County Register reasoned that the shooting was probably unprovoked because 'mob violence would not have been used' otherwise.
The Salt Lake Herald's column said the determination to lynch showed 'western civilization' short of 'Christian civilization'.
Kansas, Colorado and Montana papers reported the hanging in brief, with 'Lynch Law' and 'Strung Up to a Coal Chute' headings.
